title: Dilucidationes super methodo elegantissima, qua illustris de la Grange usus est in integranda aequatione differentiali dx/√X = dy/√Y

deep.reconstruction:
This page is the methodological preface (§§2-4) to Euler's commentary on Lagrange's integration of dx/√X = dy/√Y, where X and Y are the same general quartic (X = A+Bx+Cx²+Dx³+Ex⁴, Y the same polynomial in y). The integral being discussed, stated at the end of §1, is (√X+√Y)/(x−y) = √(Δ + D(x+y) + E(x+y)²), with Δ the arbitrary constant.

§2: Euler says he had always believed that a direct method for this equation would have to be found by looking for a suitable integrating factor. In his view every integration method falls into one of two kinds: separation of variables, or a suitable multiplier. He then names a third way, 'ipsa differentiatio', in which differentiating the equation leads to the integral. He and others had shown this in many examples. He places Lagrange's method in this third class. That is apt: Lagrange introduces an auxiliary variable t with dx/dt = √X and dy/dt = √Y. He then differentiates again, moves to the variables x+y and x−y, and obtains a second-order system that integrates at once.

§3: Euler says he will re-examine the method more carefully, adapt it to 'analytical use', and present it more simply.

§4: Lagrange's integral differs greatly from the forms Euler himself had given earlier and is much simpler, so Euler first checks that it satisfies the differential equation. He sets V = √X + √Y, so that V/(x−y) = √(Δ + D(x+y) + E(x+y)²). He squares this, so that differentiating removes Δ. The next page carries this out: V²/(x−y)² = Δ + D(x+y) + E(x+y)². Differentiating gives 2V dV/(x−y)² − 2V²(dx−dy)/(x−y)³ − (D + 2E(x+y))(dx+dy) = 0. The terms in dx and dy are then separated.

In modern terms this is a check that the algebraic curve given by Lagrange's formula is an integral curve of the Euler differential equation, i.e. the addition theorem for elliptic integrals in symmetric form.
errors: None on this page. The squaring-and-differentiating plan correctly removes Δ. (A typo on the next page, (x−y²) for (x−y)², is outside this page.)

ideas.what: Integration methods sorted into three kinds: separation of variables, integrating factor, and integration by differentiation itself
ideas.modern_name: Integration by differentiation (reduction via higher-order equations, cf. the Clairaut/d'Alembert-type technique)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler and contemporaries (Clairaut for the Clairaut equation)
ideas.where_published: Euler's Institutiones calculi integralis and various papers on integration by differentiation; exact paper numbers unsure

ideas.what: Lagrange's symmetric algebraic integral of dx/√X = dy/√Y for a general quartic
ideas.modern_name: Euler–Lagrange addition theorem for elliptic integrals
ideas.usually_credited_to: Lagrange (Miscellanea Taurinensia IV, 1766–69), building on Euler
ideas.where_published: E506 itself, Acta Acad. Sci. Petropolitanae (1778, publ. 1781); Opera omnia I.21

ideas.what: Direct check of Lagrange's integral: square, then differentiate to remove the constant Δ

deep.surprise_reason: This is a well-known paper, and the page is a historiographical preface plus the start of a routine check. Euler's attitude toward Lagrange's method and his threefold classification of integration methods are already discussed in the literature on the history of elliptic integrals.
transcription_corrections: Bottom of page: 'C 3' is the printer's signature mark and V²/(x−y)² is the catchword continuing onto p. 22; neither is part of the text.
'excedat' as printed means 'excedat' in the sense 'drops out'; it is not an error.
'quamobram' is likely a misprint or misreading of 'quamobrem'.
